lines.text: Not shown either way: studies can't yet tell whether cannabis smoke raises lung cancer risk.
Almost everyone who smoked a lot of cannabis also smoked tobacco, so the two are hard to separate.
Six studies put together found no clear difference in lung cancer between people who smoked cannabis regularly and people who didn't. A somewhat higher risk could not be ruled out.
A Swedish study followed 49,000 men for 40 years, from military call-up at age 18 to 20 until about age 60.
Men who said at call-up that they had used cannabis more than 50 times got lung cancer about twice as often, even allowing for the tobacco they smoked then.
But 91 in 100 of them also smoked tobacco, nobody asked what they smoked later in life, and at about 60 most lung cancers had not yet appeared.
Studies so far cannot tell whether smoking cannabis raises the risk of lung cancer.
Six studies put together found no clear difference, though a somewhat higher risk could not be ruled out.

A Swedish study that followed 49,000 men for 40 years found about twice the rate in men who had used cannabis more than 50 times by age 18 to 20, but almost all of them also smoked tobacco, and the study ended when the men were about 60, before most lung cancers appear.
